lessons.title: Excel for Beginners - The Complete Course
objectives: Name the parts of a spreadsheet and what each is for
Enter data so that it can be calculated on later
Decide whether to work in Excel or in Sheets
lessons.notes:
A spreadsheet is a grid where every cell holds one of three things: a number, some text, or a formula that works something out. Almost every problem beginners have comes from mixing these up.

THE PARTS: workbook, sheet, column, row, cell, and the reference that names a cell. The name box shows where you are, the formula bar shows what is really in the cell, and the two are often different - the cell shows 1,250 while the formula bar shows the calculation that produced it. Learn to look at the formula bar.

ENTER DATA SO IT CAN BE USED. One thing per cell. One row per record, one column per field, headings in the first row and nothing above them. Dates as real dates, numbers as numbers with no letters or spaces mixed in, and no blank rows in the middle of a list. A table entered properly can be sorted, filtered, summed and pivoted; the same information typed as a pretty layout can do none of those, and rebuilding it is a day of work.

NEVER STORE A NUMBER AS TEXT. If figures will not add up, this is almost always why - a stray space, a currency symbol typed in by hand, or a number pasted from a document. Module 4 covers the errors this produces.

SAVE AND SAVE AGAIN, and keep versions rather than overwriting.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - which program you should actually be learning. The course teaches Excel because that is what employers name, and the skills transfer exactly. But for most people here GOOGLE SHEETS IS THE PRACTICAL DAILY TOOL: it is free, it needs no licence paid in foreign currency, it works on a phone, it saves itself, several people can work in it at once, and it cannot be lost when a laptop dies or a flash disk is infected. Learn the thinking in either and you have both. Two specific traps when you share between them: DATES, because a sheet set to a foreign format will read 03/04 as March and a Kenyan reader means April, so set the locale before entering anything; and PHONE NUMBERS, which lose their leading zero the moment they are treated as numbers - format that column as text before you type or paste.
lessons.practice: Build one real table with proper headings, one record per row, real dates and clean numbers - a list of your own expenses for a fortnight will do. Set the file locale to Kenya, format the phone column as text, then check that the total sums correctly and that sorting by date puts the rows in true order.

quiz.question: Why must a list be entered as a proper table rather than a neat layout?
options: Only a proper table can be sorted, filtered, summed and pivoted

quiz.question: What should you do before typing phone numbers into a column?
options: Format the column as text, or the leading zero is lost

lessons.title: Google Sheets: Getting Started
objectives: Work confidently in Sheets and share a file safely
Set up a file so it survives no internet and a lost phone
Choose the right sharing permission for each person
lessons.notes:
Sheets is the same idea as Excel with the file living online. For most work here that is an advantage rather than a compromise.

WHAT YOU GET: no licence to buy, it saves every change automatically, the version history lets you go back to any earlier state, several people can edit at once, and the file is reachable from any phone or borrowed laptop. For a small business, a freelancer or a student, that combination is hard to argue with.

VERSION HISTORY IS THE FEATURE PEOPLE DISCOVER TOO LATE. Every change is recorded and any earlier version can be restored. It means a spreadsheet cannot really be destroyed by a mistake, which is exactly what makes shared files safe.

SHARING, AND THE JUDGEMENT IT NEEDS. Three levels: VIEWER can only read, COMMENTER can suggest without changing, EDITOR can change anything including deleting it. Give the lowest level that lets the person do their job. Most spreadsheets ruined in an office were ruined by someone who only needed to read them. Share with named people rather than with anyone who has the link, and when work ends, remove access rather than trusting that they will forget.

WORKING OFFLINE: switch offline access on BEFORE you need it, while you still have connection. Changes made offline sync when you reconnect.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - making this work on a Kenyan connection and a shared machine. SET OFFLINE ACCESS NOW on the files you rely on, because doing it during an outage is not possible. The PHONE APP IS FOR ENTERING AND CHECKING, not for building - type the day's sales on a phone, build the formulas on a laptop, because the phone view hides the structure and it is easy to overwrite a formula without noticing. On a shared or cyber-cafe machine, sign out properly and never tick the box that keeps you signed in. And remember that a Sheets file is only as private as its sharing setting: a link set to anyone-with-the-link that holds customer names and phone numbers is personal data exposed, which is your responsibility under the Data Protection Act, not the platform's.
lessons.practice: Take one real spreadsheet into Sheets. Turn on offline access, share it with one person as a Commenter rather than an Editor, and make a deliberate mistake then restore the previous version from history. Check the sharing settings of every file you already have and fix any set to anyone-with-the-link.

quiz.question: Which permission should you give by default?
options: The lowest level that lets the person do their job
Anyone with the link, for convenience

quiz.question: When must offline access be switched on?
options: Before you need it, while you still have connection
It is always on by default

lessons.title: Excel: Intro to Formulas
objectives: Write a formula that refers to cells rather than to typed numbers
Predict the order in which a calculation happens
Fix a formula by reading what it is actually pointing at
lessons.notes:
A formula is an instruction that works something out from other cells. The whole point is that when the underlying figures change, the answer changes by itself.

THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: REFER TO CELLS, NEVER TYPE NUMBERS INTO A FORMULA. Writing the VAT rate into fourteen formulas means fourteen edits when the rate changes, and you will miss one. Put it in a cell, point every formula at that cell, and change it once.

EVERY FORMULA STARTS WITH AN EQUALS SIGN. Without it the cell holds text that looks like a calculation and does nothing, which is a common and confusing first mistake.

ORDER OF OPERATIONS: brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. So =2+3*4 is 14, not 20. When in doubt put brackets in - they cost nothing and they make your intention readable by whoever inherits the file.

COPYING A FORMULA moves its references with it, which is usually what you want and sometimes exactly what breaks things. Module 4 covers the anchor that stops it.

READING A BROKEN FORMULA: click the cell and look at the formula bar, not at the result. The coloured outlines show which cells it is using. Nine times in ten the formula is correct and it is pointing at the wrong cells.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the habits that separate a spreadsheet people trust from one they quietly re-do by hand. Put your ASSUMPTIONS IN LABELLED CELLS at the top - the rate, the price, the margin, the exchange rate - so anyone can see and change them without opening a single formula. CHECK A FORMULA ON A ROW YOU CAN WORK OUT IN YOUR HEAD before copying it down two thousand rows. And be careful with a figure converted from another currency: store the rate in its own labelled cell with the date you took it, because a spreadsheet full of shillings converted at a forgotten rate on an unknown day is worse than no spreadsheet at all.
lessons.practice: Rebuild one calculation you currently do by hand or on a calculator. Put every assumption in a labelled cell at the top, point the formulas at those cells, and check one row by hand before copying down. Then change one assumption and confirm every figure updates.

quiz.question: Why refer to a cell instead of typing a number into a formula?
options: When the figure changes you edit one cell rather than every formula

lessons.title: Excel: Functions
objectives: Use the dozen functions that cover most real work
Choose the right function for a counting or summing question
Handle errors so a sheet stays readable
lessons.notes:
There are hundreds of functions and you need about twelve. Learn these properly rather than collecting exotic ones.

ADDING AND AVERAGING: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX. The basics, and they are most of what a working sheet does.

COUNTING: COUNT counts numbers, COUNTA counts anything that is not empty. The difference catches people out - a column of names returns zero from COUNT.

ASKING A QUESTION: IF returns one thing when a condition is true and another when it is not. This is the function that turns a list into a decision - whether an invoice is overdue, whether a stock level is low, whether a target was met.

COUNTING AND ADDING WITH A CONDITION: COUNTIF and SUMIF. How many sales in Nakuru, how much was sold in March. These two answer most of the questions a small business actually asks, and they are the point at which a spreadsheet starts saving real time.

TIDYING: ROUND to a sensible number of decimals, TRIM to remove the stray spaces that break lookups and comparisons.

DATES: TODAY gives the current date, and subtracting one date from another gives the days between - which is how you build an aged list of who owes you money and for how long.

CATCHING ERRORS: IFERROR replaces an ugly error with something readable. Use it to tidy a finished sheet, not to hide a problem you have not understood.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the two that matter most in day-to-day work here. SUMIF AND COUNTIF ARE THE PAIR TO MASTER FIRST, because the question a Kenyan small business asks is almost always how much of this, from where, in which month. And TRIM DESERVES ITS OWN HABIT: data typed by several people, or pasted from a statement or a message, is full of trailing spaces, and they are invisible. A lookup that fails for no apparent reason is a trailing space in nine cases out of ten, so clean the column before you build anything on top of it.
lessons.practice: Take one real list of transactions. Use SUMIF to total by category and COUNTIF to count them, use IF to mark anything over a threshold, and use TODAY with a date column to show how many days old each entry is. Run TRIM over any column that was typed by more than one person.

quiz.question: Which pair answers most small-business questions?
options: SUMIF and COUNTIF - how much of this, from where, in which month

quiz.question: A lookup fails for no apparent reason. What is the usual cause?
options: An invisible trailing space - clean the column with TRIM
The column is formatted as a date

lessons.title: How to Use VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP in Excel
objectives: Pull matching information from one table into another
Diagnose the four reasons a lookup returns nothing
Choose between the older and newer lookup functions
lessons.notes:
A lookup answers one question: I have a code, a name or a number here - go and find the matching row in that other table and bring back a value from it. It is the function that turns two separate lists into one useful one, and it is the skill most often tested in an interview.

VLOOKUP, which you will meet everywhere, needs four things: what to look for, where to look, which column to bring back counted from the left of that range, and - always - FALSE for an exact match. Leaving the last one off is the commonest cause of quietly wrong answers, because it then returns an approximate match without telling you.

ITS LIMITATION: it only looks to the right. The thing you search for must sit in the leftmost column of the range.

XLOOKUP, where you have it, fixes that. You give it what to look for, the column to look in, the column to return, and what to say when nothing is found. It reads more clearly, it works in any direction, and it does not break when a column is inserted.

WHY A LOOKUP RETURNS NOTHING, in the order to check:
1. The two values are not really identical - a trailing space, or different capitalisation in a place that matters.
2. ONE IS TEXT AND THE OTHER IS A NUMBER. A code typed as 00451 in one sheet and 451 in the other will never match, and this is the single commonest failure.
3. The range does not actually cover the rows you think it does, or moved when you copied the formula - anchor it.
4. The value genuinely is not there, which is a data problem and not a formula problem.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the join that matters in real Kenyan work. The everyday version of this task is MATCHING A PAYMENT LIST AGAINST A CUSTOMER LIST: an M-Pesa statement exported one way and a sales record kept another. Two things will bite you. Phone numbers appear as 0722..., +254722... and 254722... in the same job, so build one clean key column with a consistent format and look up on that rather than trying to match what you were given. And transaction codes are text, not numbers, so force both columns to text before matching. Wrap the lookup in IFERROR to show NOT FOUND rather than an error, then filter for those - the not-founds are the real work, and they are exactly what the client is paying you to find.
lessons.practice: Take two real lists that share a key - a payment list and a customer list will do. Build one clean key column in each with the same format, look up across them with an exact match, and wrap it in IFERROR to show NOT FOUND. Then filter for the not-founds and work out why each one failed.

quiz.question: What is the commonest reason a lookup finds nothing?
options: One value is text and the other is a number
The tables are on different sheets

quiz.question: Why must the last argument of VLOOKUP be FALSE?
options: Otherwise it returns an approximate match without telling you
It makes the formula calculate faster
It allows searching to the left
It is required for text values only

lessons.title: Excel Conditional Formatting Tutorial (Beginner to Pro)
objectives: Make a sheet show its own problems without being read closely
Write a rule based on a formula rather than a preset
Keep formatting useful instead of decorative
lessons.notes:
Conditional formatting colours cells according to a rule, so the sheet points at what matters instead of waiting to be studied. Used well it is the difference between a report someone reads and a report someone acts on.

WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR: overdue invoices in red, stock below the reorder level highlighted, duplicates flagged, negative numbers obvious, the highest and lowest values visible at a glance. In each case the rule answers a question the reader would otherwise have to ask.

THE PRESETS cover most needs - greater than, less than, between, text contains, duplicate values, top and bottom items, and colour scales.

THE RULE BASED ON A FORMULA is where it becomes powerful, because it can colour a whole row based on one cell. That is how you make every line of an unpaid invoice stand out rather than just the date cell. Write the condition for the first row, refer to the deciding column with its letter anchored, and apply it across the range.

THE DISCIPLINE: NO MORE THAN THREE RULES ON A SHEET, and each one meaning something. A sheet coloured in six shades communicates nothing - the eye stops distinguishing and the reader goes back to reading every cell, which is what you were trying to avoid. Use one strong colour for what needs action and leave the rest plain.

CHECK IT IN GREYSCALE, because sheets get printed, and a rule that relies on red against green is invisible both in print and to a colour-blind reader. Pair colour with a symbol or a word.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the two rules worth building into every working sheet here. First, AN AGEING RULE on anything you are owed: colour a row when today minus the invoice date passes thirty days, and again at sixty, so the sheet tells you who to ring without anyone maintaining a list. Second, A DUPLICATE RULE on the key column - repeated transaction codes or repeated phone numbers are the normal result of data typed by more than one person, and catching them at entry is far cheaper than finding them during a reconciliation. And keep the colours legible on a phone screen in daylight, since that is where most people will actually open the file.
lessons.practice: Take one working sheet and add exactly two rules: an ageing rule that colours whole rows past thirty days using a formula-based condition, and a duplicate rule on the key column. Remove any existing formatting that does not drive an action, then print a page in greyscale and check both rules are still readable.

quiz.question: Why limit a sheet to about three formatting rules?
options: Beyond that the eye stops distinguishing and the reader reads every cell anyway
Too many rules slow the file down

quiz.question: What lets a rule colour an entire row?
options: A formula-based rule referring to the deciding column with its letter anchored
